turns.text: Hey Dev. Ready to try a behavioral mock interview today?

turns.text: Yeah, let's do it. I turned in that take-home, so now I really want to practice telling my stories out loud.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: I'm stepping into the interviewer chair now. Can you tell me about a time you used data to persuade colleagues to change how they did things?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sure. Back at my school, every teacher had their own informal system for checking if students understood the daily lesson, which made it really hard to spot broader trends. I wanted our whole group to try quick end-of-class checks, but people were pretty protective of their class time.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: How did you convince them to give your idea a shot?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I decided to test it out myself first. I ran a pilot in my own classroom, and after a month, my students' weekly quiz scores jumped by ten points. When I shared that data at our department meeting, the other math teachers agreed to adopt weekly exit tickets across all their classes.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: How did you help them roll that out smoothly?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Well, some teachers worried about extra grading. So I built out basic scaffolding sheets and differentiated pacing prompts so they wouldn't spend hours on formative assessment.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: Stepping out of the interviewer role now. That's a solid story with clear results. How did that feel coming out?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It felt mostly okay, but I'm not sure if the end part landed well.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: You lean on teacher jargon like scaffolding and formative assessment that interviewers may not follow. How would you explain that prep work in plain words?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oof, yeah, you're right. I definitely fall back on school jargon like scaffolding when I talk about my past work, and an interviewer outside education probably wouldn't know what that means.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: It's an easy habit when you've taught for years. Want to try rephrasing that last piece right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, let me try. I could say I created standardized five-minute answer keys and simple score sheets so teachers could review student progress without extra overtime.

turns.speaker: wren
turns.text: That lands immediately. How did that sound in your own ears?
